## 1. Overview

This vignette walks through Bayesian estimation of the three-parameter
Exponentiated Danish (ED) submodel with `bayes_betadanish()`. The same call
with `submodel = FALSE` fits the full four-parameter Beta-Danish
distribution.

From version 1.0.0 the default sampler is the multi-chain adaptive
Metropolis algorithm used in the thesis on which the package is based. It is
written in base R, so no additional package is needed. Each chain adapts the
scale and then the shape of its proposal during the burn-in and stops
adapting before any draw is retained. The fit then reports the potential
scale reduction factor (R-hat) and the effective sample size of every
parameter, and flags the result as converged only when every R-hat is at
most 1.05 and every effective sample size is at least 400.

The single-chain sampler of earlier versions is still available as
`method = "metrop1R"`, which requires the MCMCpack and coda packages.

## 2. ED submodel on bladder cancer remission times

```{r}
library(BetaDanish)
data("remission")
fit_bayes <- bayes_betadanish(
  time     = remission$time,
  status   = remission$status,
  submodel = TRUE,
  burnin   = 2000, mcmc = 4000,
  n_chains = 4,
  seed     = 1
)
print(fit_bayes)
```

The chains start at the maximum-likelihood estimate (the first chain) and at
random perturbations of it (the others), so agreement between them is
evidence that the sampler has forgotten where it started.

## 3. Posterior diagnostics

```{r}
fit_bayes$diagnostics
fit_bayes$converged
plot(fit_bayes)
```

Each chain is drawn in its own colour in the trace panels. Chains that
overlap and show no drift are what a converged sampler looks like; the
density panels pool all chains and mark the 95% highest posterior density
interval.

## 4. Posterior survival vs Kaplan-Meier

```{r, fig.height = 4.5}
post_mean <- setNames(fit_bayes$summary$mean, fit_bayes$summary$parameter)
b <- post_mean[["b"]]; c <- post_mean[["c"]]; k <- post_mean[["k"]]
km <- survival::survfit(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = remission)
plot(km, conf.int = FALSE, xlab = "Time (months)",
     ylab = "Survival probability",
     main = "Posterior mean ED fit on remission data")
t_grid <- seq(0.1, max(remission$time), length.out = 200)
S_post <- pbetadanish(t_grid, a = 1, b = b, c = c, k = k,
                      lower.tail = FALSE)
lines(t_grid, S_post, col = "red", lwd = 2)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Kaplan-Meier", "Posterior-mean ED"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, lwd = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

## 5. Bayesian vs MLE comparison

```{r}
fit_mle <- fit_betadanish(survival::Surv(time, status) ~ 1,
                          data = remission, submodel = TRUE,
                          n_starts = 3)
cbind(
  MLE  = round(coef(fit_mle), 4),
  Bayes_post_mean = round(post_mean[names(coef(fit_mle))], 4)
)
```

## 6. The four-parameter model

For the full model the posterior of the product `a * c` is usually far better
determined than those of `a` and `c` separately, because near the lower tail
the two enter the density almost only through their product. The summary
therefore carries an extra row, `a_times_c`. The four-parameter posterior
needs longer chains than the ED one; check `converged` before using it.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_bd <- bayes_betadanish(remission$time, remission$status,
                           submodel = FALSE, burnin = 20000, mcmc = 40000,
                           seed = 1)
fit_bd$summary
fit_bd$converged
```
